headline: Why Some A.I. Evangelists Aren’t Bothered by the Potential for Human Extinction

paragraphs.text: On Nov. 19, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief executive, Dario Amodei, rang the Nasdaq bell to announce, to great fanfare, an initial public offering of tech millenarianism. Almost instantly, the company’s 5,000 employees became collectively richer than the poorest 100 million Americans combined. Six hundred of them were minted centimillionaires.

The offering wasn’t an unmitigated success, with share prices tumbling shortly after opening. Even so, it was a remarkable, trillion-dollar affirmation for a company founded just five years earlier, during the pandemic emergency, by a band of reluctant capitalists terrified by the prospect of out-of-control A.I. progress. As recently as last year, Amodei was estimating the chances that artificial intelligence would bring about human extinction at between 10 and 25 percent. Anthropic’s own I.P.O. filings acknowledged that its product might cause catastrophic or even existential harms and projected that the entire global insurance industry might not be big enough to cover that risk.

By now, warnings like these have become crazily familiar. Even Trump’s former tech czar, the A.I. pollyanna David Sacks, has called work on recursive self-improvement — in which A.I. essentially trains itself — the most dangerous thing anyone could be doing. At Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg’s blasé materialism has long prevailed, the wunderkind A.I. lead, Alexandr Wang, warned in late November that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control.” Paul Christiano, who joined the OpenAI board in September, told a large audience this month that A.I. accidents would be the most likely cause of death for most people in the room. And Buck Shlegeris, chief executive of the A.I. security company Redwood Research, said he thinks “there’s a very real possibility (maybe 20 percent) that within a year, A.I. misalignment issues prevent you from going about life normally, because you are dead or enslaved.”

Ever since ChatGPT first tugged Silicon Valley’s machine-god dreams into public view in 2022, the obvious question has gone unnervingly unanswered: Why would so many people who believe artificial intelligence could perhaps bring about human extinction nevertheless be racing so fast to build it?

The tsunami of A.I.-related wealth offers one cynical explanation. Those on the inside offer others: an urgent arms race, with other companies or with China; the possibility of superabundance; the need to bend technological history in a somewhat more humane direction.

But to the list I would add another one: that some number of A.I. accelerationists remain unbothered by the possibility of extinction or human obsolescence because they don’t believe it would be a bad outcome, necessarily. On some level, on some timeline, they consider it inevitable. Often, even, a source of enthralling awe.

For decades, the practical work of Silicon Valley was shaped spiritually by what became known as the “California ideology,” a mix of hippy counterculture, live-and-let-live libertarianism and market-friendly technological determinism.

Today the vibe is closer to religious fervor, with a proliferation of new creeds often tending toward the eschatological. One variety is called “successionism”: the belief that, in building artificial intelligence, humanity’s most gifted technologists are giving rise to an entirely new species, destined to rule by sheer force of superintelligence and sidelining measly human minds. Elon Musk has long called humanity merely a “biological bootloader” for what’s to follow; the writer and philosopher Ginevra Davis has imagined a near future in which it has become clear that the “cosmic purpose” of our species was merely to mine silicon. “Human extinction would be a profound tragedy,” the A.I. researcher Daniel Faggella wrote the week before the Anthropic I.P.O., reflecting on the possibility of rapid A.I. takeoff. “But something even greater is at stake.”

For normies, these may be the most cosmically unnerving features of A.I. — that the technology could bring about cognitive obsolescence and the end of the human era. (To trust the march of whistle-blowers, perhaps quite quickly.) But in Silicon Valley, the ideas are neither all that unusual nor all that new, having developed over many decades of slower and less visible A.I. progress. Then things accelerated, with spectacularly well-funded visionaries finally building something resembling their dreams and nightmares. And they became, as a result, the fabulously wealthy, immensely powerful architects of our collective future — a new class of tech overlords with a pretty distinctive way of seeing the world and their own place in the long arc of human history.

In 2023, the A.I. researcher Timnit Gebru and the philosopher Émile Torres — two spiky critics of big A.I. who are not exactly beloved in Silicon Valley — described this emergent worldview as the “TESCREAL bundle,” an acronym that folded seven distinct but related intellectual strands into a single package of apocalyptic techno-futurism. The resulting bundle isn’t a precise ideological map so much as a broadly illustrative mood board.

First is transhumanism, the belief that humans can and should find ways of evolving past their biological limitations. The second is extropianism, which involves extending human control over more and more of the physical universe. Singularitarianism proposes that exponential technological progress will soon reach takeoff and bring humanity into an unknowable future. Cosmism is a modern variant of 19th-century Russian alchemistic science aimed at achieving human immortality, invoked by Peter Thiel, among others. Rationalism is a rigorous debate-society approach to making quasi-mathematical judgments about the world. Effective altruism is an ethically demanding do-gooder approach to the survival and well-being of those elsewhere around the world — which evolved to emphasize the ethical and moral value of animal and plant life. Then there is the final piece of the bundle: longtermism, which suggests that stewardship of the future should be our central political and ethical goal in the blighted present.

Not everyone working in artificial intelligence believes that the world as we know it may be about to end or that recursive self-improvement is right around the corner, or that, even if it does come soon, it will necessarily prove quite so transformative. But the sense of imminent obsolescence hangs in the air like a Bay Area fog, seeping into the thinking of hardheaded materialists and even A.I. optimists, too. But for outsiders the utopian visions (thousand-year life spans, economic superabundance) can look pretty dystopian (loss of individual autonomy, the end of politics, perhaps an A.I. welfare state to support all the layabout humans).

The genomics researcher and writer Ruxandra Teslo has called this worldview “handoverism”: that short of extinction, humans will inevitably hand over control of everything to robots and machine intelligence, choosing a kind of petlike existence for ourselves and celebrating it all as transcendence.

The A.I. philosopher Dean Ball, who helped design the Trump administration’s A.I. policy in 2025, calls handoverism the “silent consensus” of the industry: that intelligence is all that matters; that a new and awe-inspiring form of it is now emerging, in what is best understood as a kind of evolutionary leap; that its future capabilities lie so far beyond our Stone Age brains we can’t predict the shape of what’s to come; and that the sheer power of A.I. promises to overwhelm anything humans might muster to resist or even direct it. Perhaps it will bring about the end of all human disease, as Amodei has predicted (a possibility that almost all biological researchers have dismissed). Perhaps it would bring about a crisis of human meaning, of the kind now sweeping the world of mathematics after A.I. produced several previously unimaginable breakthroughs in the span of a few months. “Regardless of the specifics,” Ball writes, the silent consensus means “the termination of human primacy in the world as we know it.”

Religious revivals need not be truly universal to illuminate their age. That is why we study the Black Death in part through the penitential response of medieval Christians, why the Reformation tells you something about Europe in the age of the printing press, why Mormonism and Methodism reveal some things about industrialization and the closing of the American frontier and why the prosperity gospel emerges tellingly in the United States of the late 20th century. And as much as A.I. millenarianism reflects features of the technology itself, it also reflects something about the world in which those tools have landed — namely the widespread feeling of social disempowerment already pervading our politics.

No country has invested more in artificial intelligence than the United States, which has spent five times as much as China, our nominal rival. No country is more anxious about the technology than we are. In China, A.I. anxieties have been kept in check by widespread faith that Beijing would intervene in any crisis to ensure social stability and the continuation of the regime. But no nation trusts its government to monitor A.I. less than the United States, where citizens are panicking about breakouts of A.I. agent swarms and widespread I.T. outages have reached crisis levels. We’ve recently watched the White House bully the world’s second-most-valuable company, Nvidia, to ignore blaring national-security alarms and reinstall its scandal-plagued chief executive, Jensen Huang, to rescue a crashing stock market.

The public has recoiled from all this and is fighting back. By wide margins, Americans believe that the technology will do more harm than good, with typically fewer than 10 percent telling pollsters they are very enthusiastic. Nearly three-quarters of the country opposes the construction of data centers — a coalition so much larger than other NIMBY alliances against more obviously noxious construction projects that the near-unanimity must reflect broader rage about the machine future. And in the midterm elections, Democrats used the threat of A.I. turbulence and the menace of tech oligarchs as the binding agent for a new crusade against plutocracy and corruption — contributing to a stomping victory.

But in certain ways these protests mirror the logic of their opposition. Like all good science fiction, the basic story of A.I. takeover echoes widespread contemporary anxieties: that we are already, in many waves, slaves to technology and becoming more so; that our political economy is already broken; that we have already handed over much of our lives to forces beyond our control; and that so much of the culture and institutions that might have once seemed to offer comfort and stability in the face of social turbulence now stands so obviously degraded, like ruins from another era.
The question is: Who rules the next one?
